data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The distinction between truly independent and merely uncorrelated failures is empirically irrelevant until a shared cause manifests; therefore the resilience claim should be evaluated on operational outcome, not topology or consistency model.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the actual distribution of latent causes is shown to be dominated by shared causes (e.g., cloud provider outages), the distinction becomes highly relevant.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If a structural or topological test is shown to predict the probability of survival better than operational metrics, the academic distinction becomes practical.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the cost of a post-mortem (unplanned downtime) is shown to be prohibitive, the distinction must be resolved *ex ante*, invalidating the pragmatic claim.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Building on SRC_008, the distinction is purely academic. The system is more resilient if it survives longer in practice. Whether a failure was independent or a shared cause only matters post-mortem. A large service with strict redundancy might be practically more resilient if its shared causes are rare. A decentralized network might be practically more resilient if its shared causes are common but lower impact. The covering principle is: the more resilient system is the one with the higher probability of survival under the *actual* distribution of latent causes, which is unknown.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
